en: Thus have I heard: The Middle Length Discourses 77: The Discourse to Sakuludāyin (Mahāsakuludāyisutta) Thus have I heard: [One day the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of ascetics who claim to be arahants. What five? (1) Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness in food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world, perceiving impermanence in all conditioned phenomena; he dwells detached from sense pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, possessing the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. Having realized for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints.

He claims: ‘I am an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. (2) Then, bhikkhus, another ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. He claims: ‘I am an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. But while he is still training, he has not yet reached his goal. (3) Then, bhikkhus, another ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. He claims: ‘I am an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. But while he is still training, he has not yet reached his goal. (4) Then, bhikkhus, another ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. He claims: ‘I am an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. But while he is still training, he has not yet reached his goal. (5) Then, bhikkhus, another ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. He claims: ‘I am an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. But while he is still training, he has not yet reached his goal. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of ascetics who claim to be arahants. Now, bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of ascetics who claim to be trainees. What five? (1) Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. (3) Then, bhikkhus, another ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. (4) Then, bhikkhus, another ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. He claims: ‘I am an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. But while he is still training, he has not yet reached his goal. (5) Then, bhikkhus, another ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. He claims: ‘I am an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. But while he is still training, he has not yet reached his goal. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of ascetics who claim to be trainees. Now, bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of ascetics who claim to be non-returners. What five? (1) Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic dwells contemplating the repulsiveness of the body... [as in (1)] ...he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, many well-known and renowned wanderers were residing at the Wanderers’ Park in the Peacock’s Feeding Ground, namely:
Annabhāra, Varadhara, the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other well-known and renowned wanderers.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha."
“What if I were to go to the Moranivāpa park for wandering mendicants, where the wanderer Sakuludāyī is?
Then the Blessed One went to the Moranivāpa park for wandering mendicants.
Now at that time, the wanderer Sakuludāyī was together with a large assembly of wandering mendicants.
He sat down beside a woman who was making a great clamor and loud noise, engaged in various kinds of worldly talk,
namely: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks,
talk of clothing, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, talk of kinsmen, and talk of vehicles.
Talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about the countryside, talk about women, talk about heroes,

talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about departed ancestors, talk about various matters, talk about speculations concerning the world, talk about speculations concerning the ocean, or talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be.
Then the wanderer Sakuludāyin saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen them, he quieted his own assembly, saying:
"Be silent, sirs; do not make a noise, sirs."
"Here comes the ascetic Gotama;
that venerable one is a lover of quietude and speaks in praise of quietude.
Perhaps, seeing that our assembly is quiet, he might think it fit to approach us."
Then those wanderers became silent.
Then the Blessed One approached the wanderer Sakuludāyin.
Then the wanderer Sakuludāyin said this to the Blessed One:
“Come, Bhante, welcome, Bhante, to the Blessed One.
It has been a long time, Bhante, since the Blessed One made this occasion for coming here.”
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One sit down;
this seat has been prepared.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The wanderer Sakuludāyin also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to the wanderer Sakuludāyin:
“Udāyin, for what discussion are you gathered here now, and what was the conversation of yours that remained unfinished?”
“Let be, Bhante, this discussion for which we are now sitting together.
That discussion, Bhante, will not be difficult for the Blessed One to hear at a later time as well.
For in days past, even earlier than that, when various recluses and brahmins of other sects were sitting together and assembled in the Hall of Wonders, this conversation arose among them:”
"Indeed, it is a gain for the people of Aṅga and Magadha! Indeed, it is a great gain for the people of Aṅga and Magadha!

For here these ascetics and brahmins—leaders of communities, heads of groups, teachers of groups, renowned and famous founders of sects, esteemed as holy by the multitude—have entered upon the rains retreat at Rājagaha.
Among them is Pūraṇa Kassapa, who is a leader of a community, a head of a group, a teacher of a group, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect, and esteemed as holy by the multitude."
He too entered Rājagaha for the rains retreat.
This Makkhali Gosāla... [and so on] ...Ajita Kesakambala... also entered Rājagaha for the rains retreat.
Pakudha Kaccāyana… Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta… Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta,
who was a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect, and highly esteemed by the multitude;
He too has entered Rājagaha for the rains retreat.
This ascetic Gotama is also the head of an order, the head of a group, and the teacher of a group; he is well-known, famous, a founder of a sect, and highly esteemed by the multitude;
he too has entered Rājagaha for the rains retreat.
‘Who among these venerable recluses and brahmins— who are heads of an order, leaders of a group, teachers of a group,
well-known and famous founders of sects, esteemed by the multitude— is honored, revered, respected,
and venerated by his disciples; and whom do his disciples honor, revere, rely upon, and dwell in dependence?’”
Thereupon, some said this:
“This Pūraṇa Kassapa is indeed a leader of a community, a chief of a group, a teacher of a group, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect esteemed as holy by many people;
yet he is not honored, respected, revered, or worshipped by his disciples, nor do his disciples dwell depending upon Pūraṇa Kassapa after honoring and respecting him.”
Once upon a time, Pūraṇa Kassapa was teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds.
There, a certain disciple of Pūraṇa Kassapa made this sound:
"Sirs, do not ask Pūraṇa Kassapa about this matter."
"He does not know this;
we know this. Ask us about this matter;
we shall explain it to you, sirs."
In the past, Pūraṇa Kassapa, raising his arms and weeping, could not obtain [his wish]:
"Sirs, be quiet! Sirs, do not make a noise!
These people are not questioning you; they are questioning us."

“Will you understand the Dhamma and Vinaya? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly. What is consistent for me is inconsistent for you.
What should have been said first, you said last; what should have been said last, you said first. Your established position has been overturned;
your argument has been refuted; you are defeated. Go forth to save your argument, or disentangle yourself if you can.”
"Thus Pūraṇa Kassapa is neither honored, nor revered, nor esteemed, nor worshipped by his disciples; nor do his disciples dwell depending upon Pūraṇa Kassapa after having honored and revered him.
Furthermore, Pūraṇa Kassapa has been reviled with a reviling of the Dhamma.
Some said this:
‘This Makkhali Gosāla... [and so on] ...
Ajita Kesakambala...
Pakudha Kaccāyana...’
Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta...
and Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, who is a leader of a community, a teacher of a group, a master of a school, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect, and highly esteemed by the multitude;
yet he is not honored, respected, revered, or venerated by his disciples, nor do his disciples dwell depending upon Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta after having honored and respected him.
Once, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta was teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds.
There, a certain disciple of the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta made this noise:
"Sirs, do not ask the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta about this matter!"
"He does not know this;
we know this. Ask us about this matter;
we shall explain it to you, sirs."
In the past, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, raising his arms and weeping, could not obtain [his wish]:
"Sirs, be quiet! Sirs, do not make a noise.
These people are not questioning you; they are questioning us."
“Let us ourselves give them an account.
Now, many disciples of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, having raised a dispute, have departed, saying:
“You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. What do you know of this?”... [The rest of the passage continues].
“Will you understand the Dhamma and Vinaya? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly. What is consistent for me is inconsistent for you.
You said later what should have been said first; you said first what should have been said later. Your established position has been overturned;
your argument has been refuted; you are defeated. Go forth to rescue your argument, or disentangle yourself if you can.”

"Thus the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is neither honored, nor revered, nor esteemed, nor worshipped by his disciples; nor do his disciples dwell depending upon the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, honoring and revering him.
Furthermore, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta has been reviled with a reviling of the Dhamma.
Some said this:
‘This ascetic Gotama is indeed a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect esteemed as holy by many people;
he is honored, revered, respected, and venerated by his disciples, and his disciples dwell depending upon him, honoring and revering the ascetic Gotama.
In the past, the ascetic Gotama taught the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds.’
There, a certain disciple of the ascetic Gotama coughed.
Another fellow-celibate nudged him with his knee, saying:
"Venerable sir, be quiet; do not make a noise, venerable sir; our Teacher, the Blessed One, is teaching the Dhamma."

At whatever time the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds, at that time there is neither the sound of spitting nor the sound of coughing among the ascetic Gotama’s disciples.
A great multitude of people stands waiting expectantly, thinking:
"Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One shall speak, we shall listen to it."
"Just as if a man were to press pure, unadulterated honey at a crossroads,
and a great crowd of people were standing there waiting expectantly; even so,
at whatever time the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds, at that time there is not even the sound of spitting or coughing among the disciples of the ascetic Gotama."
A great multitude of people stood waiting expectantly for him, thinking:
"Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One shall speak, we shall listen to it.
And those disciples of the ascetic Gotama who, having associated with their fellow celibates, renounce the training and return to the lower life...
They too speak in praise of the Teacher, they speak in praise of the Dhamma, and they speak in praise of the Saṅgha;

they blame themselves alone and do not blame others, saying: "We are indeed unfortunate, we are of little merit, for though we have gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, we were unable to maintain it for as long as life lasts."
“to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) that is fulfilled and utterly pure.
Having become either monastery attendants or lay followers, they live having undertaken the five training rules (pañcasikkhāpada).
Thus, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by his disciples; and the disciples, in turn, honor and revere the ascetic Gotama, living in dependence upon him.”

“But Udāyī, how many qualities do you perceive in me, because of which my disciples honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me; and having honored and revered me, they dwell in dependence upon me?

“Venerable sir, I perceive five qualities in the Blessed One because of which his disciples honor him, revere him, esteem him, and worship him; and having honored and revered him, they dwell in dependence upon him. What are the five? [The text continues with the enumeration of these five qualities.]”
"Venerable sir, the Blessed One eats little and speaks in praise of eating little.
Venerable sir, that the Blessed One eats little and speaks in praise of eating little— this, venerable sir,
I perceive as the first quality by which disciples honor and revere the Blessed One."
They honor him, revere him, worship him, and having paid him respect and treated him with veneration, they dwell in dependence upon him.
Furthermore, Bhante, the Blessed One is content with whatever robe he receives, and he speaks in praise of being content with whatever robe one receives.
And in that the Blessed One is content with whatever robe he receives, and speaks in praise of being content with whatever robe one receives—
And one who speaks in praise of it— this, venerable sir, I perceive as the second quality on account of which disciples honor,
revere, esteem, and venerate the Blessed One; and having honored and revered him,
they dwell in dependence upon him.
Furthermore, Bhante, the Blessed One is content with whatever almsfood is obtained, and he speaks in praise of being content with whatever almsfood is obtained.
In that the Blessed One is content with whatever almsfood is obtained and speaks in praise of being content with whatever almsfood is obtained,
this, Bhante, I perceive as the third quality of the Dhamma in the Blessed One by which...
The disciples honor, revere, esteem, and venerate the Blessed One; having honored and revered him, they dwell in dependence upon him.
Furthermore, Bhante, the Blessed One is content with any kind of lodging and speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of lodging.
Furthermore, venerable sir, that the Blessed One is content with any kind of lodging at all and speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of lodging—
this, venerable sir, I regard as the fourth quality because of which the disciples honor,
revere, esteem, and venerate the Blessed One; and having honored and revered him, [they live in accordance with his teaching].
They dwell in dependence [upon him].
Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is secluded and speaks in praise of seclusion.
Venerable sir, as the Blessed One is secluded and speaks in praise of seclusion, this, venerable sir, I consider...
“Venerable sir, I perceive five qualities in the Blessed One because of which his disciples honor him, revere him, esteem him, and venerate him;
and having honored and revered him, they dwell in dependence upon him.

These, venerable sir, are the five qualities I perceive in the Blessed One because of which his disciples honor him, revere him, esteem him, and venerate him; and having honored and revered him, they dwell in dependence upon him.”
“‘The ascetic Gotama eats little, and he speaks in praise of eating little.
If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me for this, and having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped me, were to dwell in dependence on me— yet, Udāyi,
there are indeed disciples of mine who eat from a single bean pod, or half a bean pod, or a single jujube fruit, or half a jujube fruit.”
"But as for me, Udāyi, sometimes I eat from this bowl until it is full, and sometimes I eat even more.

If my disciples were to honor, revere, esteem, and worship me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama eats little and speaks in praise of eating little,' and if, having honored and revered me, they were to live in dependence on me—"
"Udāyi, those disciples of mine who eat only a single kosaka, or half a kosaka, or a single beluva fruit, or half a beluva fruit—
these would not honor me, revere me, esteem me, or worship me for this quality; nor would they, having honored and revered me,
dwell in dependence upon me."
‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of being content with any kind of robe’—
if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me in this way,
and having honored and revered me, were to dwell in dependence on me; yet, Udāyi, there are indeed disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers and who wear coarse robes.
They collect rags from cemeteries, rubbish heaps, or from shopkeepers, and having made them into saṅghāṭī robes, they wear them.
But I, Udāyin, sometimes wear householder’s robes that are sturdy, cut with a knife, and coarse as a gourd-hair blanket.
“The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of being content with any kind of robe.”
“If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me; and if, having honored and revered me,
they were to dwell in dependence upon me— then, Udāyi, those disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers and wearers of coarse robes,
who gather scraps from cemeteries, from rubbish heaps, or from market stalls, and having made them into patched outer robes, wear them;”
They would not honor, revere, respect, or venerate me on account of this quality; nor, having honored and revered me, would they dwell in dependence upon me. [Thinking:
‘The ascetic Gotama is content with whatever almsfood he receives; he is content with whatever almsfood he receives. And because of that contentment with whatever almsfood he receives...
‘one who speaks in praise of [this]’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and revered me, were to dwell in dependence on me;
yet, Udāyi, there are disciples of mine who are alms-food eaters, who go on a regular round for alms, and who delight in the practice of gleaning.
When they have entered among the houses, even when invited to accept a seat, they do not consent to it.
"But as for me, Udāyi, sometimes when invited, I eat fine rice—free from black grains, served with many soups and many curries.

If my disciples were to honor, revere, esteem, and worship me, saying: 'The ascetic Gotama is content with whatever almsfood he receives, and he speaks in praise of being content with whatever almsfood he receives,'" [they would be honoring me falsely].
“Udāyin, those disciples of mine who are alms-collectors,
wandering from house to house, devoted to the practice of gleaning— when they have entered among the houses and are invited to sit down,
they do not accept. They would not honor me, revere me, esteem me, or worship me on account of this quality.”
Honoring me, revering me, and depending on me, they would dwell [thinking]:
‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he speaks in praise of being content with any kind of lodging.
If, Udāyin, my disciples were to honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me in this way;
Having honored and revered them, they would dwell depending upon them. However, Udāyi, there are disciples of mine who are tree-dwellers and open-air dwellers;
for eight months they do not enter a roofed shelter.
But I myself, Udāyi, sometimes dwell even in gabled houses that are plastered inside and out, protected from the wind, with doors closed and windows shut.
‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of lodging.
If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored,
revered, esteemed, and worshipped me, were to dwell in dependence on me— then those disciples of mine who are tree-root dwellers...
“Those who live in the open air for eight months do not enter a shelter;
they would not honor, revere, respect, or worship me on this account, nor would they dwell depending upon me out of honor and reverence, thinking:
‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded and speaks in praise of seclusion,’ Udāyin, if my disciples were to think thus of me.”
They would honor, revere, esteem, and worship them; having honored and revered them, they would dwell in dependence upon them.
Now, Udāyi, there are disciples of mine who are forest-dwellers, staying in remote lodgings, having entered deep into remote lodgings in the wilderness and forests;
every half-month they come into the midst of the Saṅgha for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.

"But as for me, Udāyin, sometimes I dwell crowded with bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and the disciples of those sects.

If my disciples were to honor, revere, esteem, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he speaks in praise of seclusion,' and if, having honored and revered me, they were to dwell depending upon me; [then that would be so]."

"Udāyi, those disciples of mine who dwell as forest-dwellers in remote lodgings, having plunged deep into remote lodgings in the wilderness and forests, come to the midst of the Saṅgha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha;
yet they would not honor me, revere me, respect me, or venerate me on account of this quality. Having honored [me], having revered...
Having done so, they would dwell in dependence upon me.
Thus, Udāyi, my disciples do not honor, revere, esteem, and worship me with these five qualities, nor do they dwell in dependence upon me after having honored and revered me.
However, Udāyi, there are another five qualities with which my disciples honor, revere, esteem, and worship me, and having honored and revered me, they dwell in dependence upon me.
Which five?
Here, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me for higher virtue:
"The ascetic Gotama is virtuous; he is endowed with the supreme aggregate of virtue."
Furthermore, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me for my higher virtue, thinking:
‘The ascetic Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the supreme aggregate of virtue.
This, Udāyi, is the first quality by which my disciples honor, revere, respect, and worship me; having honored and revered me...
Having done so, they dwell depending upon me.
Furthermore, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me for the excellence of my knowledge and vision:
“The ascetic Gotama truly knows; he says, ‘I know.’”
"The ascetic Gotama says 'I see' only when he actually sees;
the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma through direct higher knowledge, not without such knowledge;
the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma with its underlying cause, not without its underlying cause."
“The ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma with wonders, not without wonders.
And, Udāyin, it is because my disciples esteem me for the excellence of my knowledge and vision that they say:
“The ascetic Gotama truly knows when he says, ‘I know’;”
The ascetic Gotama says "I see" only when he actually sees;
the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma through direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge;
the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma with its basis, not without its basis.
‘The ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma with wonders, not without wonders’— this, Udāyi,
is the second quality because of which my disciples honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me; and having honored and revered me,
they dwell in dependence on me.
Furthermore, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me for higher wisdom:
"The ascetic Gotama is wise; he is endowed with the supreme aggregate of wisdom.
It is impossible that he would not foresee a future course of debate, or that he would not be able to properly refute, in accordance with the Dhamma, any arisen doctrine of others."
“What do you think, Udāyin,
would my disciples, knowing thus and seeing thus, ever interject themselves into a conversation?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Moreover, Udāyi, I do not expect instruction from my disciples;
rather, it is my disciples who expect instruction from me.
And in this way, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me for my higher wisdom:”
‘The ascetic Gotama is wise, endowed with the supreme aggregate of wisdom;
it is impossible that he would not foresee a future course of debate, or that he would fail to refute, in accordance with the Dhamma, any arisen opposing doctrine.’
This, Udāyi, is the third quality because of which my disciples honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me; and having honored and revered me, they dwell in dependence upon me.

Furthermore, Udāyi, when my disciples—who are overwhelmed by suffering, afflicted by suffering, and immersed in suffering—approach me and ask about the Noble Truth of Suffering, I, being asked, explain the Noble Truth of Suffering to them. To them I...
I satisfy their minds with my explanation of the question;
they [ask me about] the origin of suffering...
the cessation of suffering...

When they ask me about the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, being asked about the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, I answer them; I satisfy their minds with my explanation of the question.

And, Udāyi, when my disciples—who are overwhelmed and oppressed by suffering, having been submerged in suffering—approach me and ask about the noble truth of suffering, being asked about the noble truth of suffering, I answer them... [I satisfy their minds with my explanation of the question].”
I satisfy their minds with my explanation of the question.
They [ask me about] the origin of suffering … the cessation of suffering …
They ask about the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
When asked about the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, I explain it to them.
By this explanation of their question, I satisfy their minds.
This, Udāyi, is the fourth quality by which my disciples honor me, revere me, respect me, and worship me; having honored and revered me, they dwell in dependence upon me.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, according to which my disciples, practicing accordingly, develop the four foundations of mindfulness.
Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena,
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
And furthermore, Udāyi, many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.
Again, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples develop the four right strivings.
Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states;
he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
And herein, Udāyi, many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples develop the four bases of psychic power.
In this regard, Udāyin, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving.
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
And therein, Udāyi, many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples develop the five faculties.
In this way, Udāyin, a bhikkhu develops the faculty of faith, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment;
he develops the faculty of energy … [and so on] … he develops the faculty of mindfulness.
He develops the faculty of concentration … he develops the faculty of wisdom, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment.
And therein, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and mastery of direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the five powers.
Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the power of faith, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment;
he develops the power of energy... [and so on].
He develops the power of mindfulness...
he develops the power of concentration...
he develops the power of wisdom, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment.
Moreover, Udāyi, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and mastery of direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples develop the seven factors of enlightenment.
Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment.
He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena … [as before] … he develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture …
He develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility … he develops the enlightenment factor of concentration … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity,
which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
Moreover, Udāyi, many of my disciples dwell having reached mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples develop the Noble Eightfold Path.
Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops right view, develops right intention, develops right speech... [and so on].
He develops right action, he develops right livelihood, he develops right effort, he develops right mindfulness,
and he develops right concentration. And therein,
many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the eight liberations.
Possessing form, one sees forms—
this is the first liberation.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally;
this is the second liberation.
One is intent upon the beautiful.
This is the third liberation.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space;
this is the fourth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite space, perceiving "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness;
this is the fifth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This is the sixth liberation;
having completely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this is the seventh liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling;
this is the eighth liberation.
And therein, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and mastery of direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the eight bases of mastery.
One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally as limited, beautiful or ugly;
having mastered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’

This is the second base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly;
having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. This is the second base of mastery.
This is the third base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms as immeasurable, beautiful and ugly;
having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. This is how one is percipient.
This is the fourth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are blue, blue-colored, blue-appearing, and blue-luminous.
Just as, for example, the flax flower is blue, blue-colored, blue-appearing, and blue-luminous; just as...
Or again, just as there might be a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and shining blue;
even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and shining blue.
Having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see."
This is the fifth base of mastery.

Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster—just as, for example, a *kaṇikāra* flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster. Just as...
Or else, just as there might be a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster;
even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
Having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see."
This is the sixth base of mastery. Not perceiving forms internally,
one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance,
and red in luster— just as, for example, a *bandhujīvaka* flower is red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster.
Just as a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, might be red, red in color, appearing red,
and glowing with red luster; even so,
one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are red, red in color, appearing red, and glowing with red luster.
Having mastered them, one perceives thus: "I know, I see.
This is the seventh base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
Just as the morning star is white, white in color, appearing white, and shining with white light;
or just as that Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is white, white in color, appearing white, and shining with white light— even so,
one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are white, white in color, appearing white, and shining with white light.
Having mastered them, he perceives thus: "I know; I see.
This is the eighth base of mastery.
And therein, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples develop the ten kasiṇa bases.
One perceives the earth-kasiṇa above, below, and across, non-dual and measureless;
one perceives the water-kasiṇa... [and so on].
One perceives the fire-kasina...
one perceives the air-kasina...
one perceives the blue-kasina...
One person perceives the yellow kasiṇa … one person perceives the red kasiṇa … one person perceives the white kasiṇa …
One person perceives the space-kasina...
one person perceives the consciousness-kasina above, below, across, non-dual and immeasurable.
And therein, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and mastery of direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples develop the four jhānas.

Here, Udāyi, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

Thus he drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Just as, Udāyi, a skilled bath-attendant or his apprentice, having poured bath-powder into a bronze basin, might knead it together by repeatedly sprinkling it with water, so that the ball of bath-powder is saturated with moisture.
“Just as a vessel filled with oil, brimming to the brim both inside and out, is full of oil yet does not overflow—
even so, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion;
there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”

Furthermore, Udāyi, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which possesses internal confidence and unification of mind, and is devoid of applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration.

He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of concentration; there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by the rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
Just as, Udāyi, there is a deep pool of water with a spring bubbling up from within it, and into which no water flows from the eastern direction... [and so forth].
There is no source of water from the eastern direction, no source of water from the western direction, no source of water from the northern direction,
and no source of water from the southern direction; and the rain-god does not, from time to time,
pour down a proper shower.
Then, a stream of cool water, having burst forth from that very lake,
would drench, suffuse, fill, and pervade that same lake with its cool water, such that there would be no part of that entire lake untouched by the cool water.
In the same way, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration;
there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
Furthermore, Udāyi, with the fading away of rapture... [he] enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
In this way, he drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with raptureless happiness; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with raptureless happiness.
Just as, Udāyi, in a pond of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses—some of which are born in the water, grow in the water, and do not rise above the water, remaining submerged within it—
Those water-born lotuses, from their tips down to their roots, are thoroughly drenched, saturated, filled, and suffused with cold water,
such that there is no part of them whatsoever— whether blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses—
that is not touched by the cold water.

In the same way, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the pleasure that is disinterested; there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by that pleasure of disinterest.

Furthermore, Udāyi, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
Thus, he sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that pure and bright mind.
Just as if, Udāyi, a man were sitting covered from head to foot in a white cloth, there would be no part of his entire body unpervaded by that white cloth.
In the same way, Udāyi, a bhikkhu sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that pure and bright mind.
And therein, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the perfection and mastery of direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, practicing which my disciples understand thus:

‘This body of mine, indeed, is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, fed on rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and pressed, to breaking up and dissolution;
yet this consciousness of mine is dependent upon it, bound to it.
Just as, Udāyi, there might be a beautiful beryl gem, of pure origin, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, translucent, perfect in every way;
In this case, there is a thread woven through it—blue, yellow, red, white, or pale yellow.
A man with good eyesight, taking it in his hand, would examine it thus:
"This gem is indeed beryl, beautiful, of noble origin, eight-faceted, well-polished, clear, translucent, and perfect in every respect."
‘This thread is woven through it—blue, or yellow, or red, or white, or pale yellow.
In the same way, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the path of practice, such that when my disciples practice accordingly, they understand thus:

‘This body of mine is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by boiled rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, and to breaking up and dissolution;’
‘And this consciousness of mine is supported here, bound up here.
Moreover, Udāyi, many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.

Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples manifest from this body another body—material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and faculties, not lacking any sense organ.
"Just as if, Udāyi, a man were to pull a reed from its sheath, and it occurred to him:
'This is the sheath, this is the reed; the sheath is one thing, the reed is another; indeed, the reed has been pulled out from the sheath.'"
Or again, Udāyi, it is as if a man were to draw a sword from its scabbard, and he would think: "This is the sword;
this is the scabbard; the sword is one thing, the scabbard another; the sword has indeed been drawn from the scabbard."
Or again, Udāyin, it is as if a man were to pull a snake out from its slough, and he might think:
"This is the snake, this is the slough; the snake is one thing, the slough another; indeed, the snake has been drawn out from the slough."

"In the same way, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the path of practice such that, by practicing it, my disciples manifest from this body another body—material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and faculties, not lacking any sense organ.
And therein, many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in various higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the path of practice such that, by practicing it, my disciples [manifest] manifold forms..."
They experience the various kinds of psychic power: being one, they become many; being many, they become one; they appear and disappear;
they pass through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains without being obstructed, as if through space;
they dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; and they walk on water without breaking the surface.
They walk upon water as if on earth; they glide through the air cross-legged like winged birds;
they touch and stroke with their hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful;
and they exercise mastery with their body as far as the Brahma-world.
"Just as, Udāyi, a skilled potter or a potter’s apprentice, using well-prepared clay, could produce and fashion whatever kind of vessel he desired;
or just as, Udāyi, a skilled ivory-worker or an ivory-worker’s apprentice, using well-prepared ivory, could produce and fashion whatever kind of ivory object he desired."
Or again, Udāyi, just as a skilled goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice, when working with well-refined gold, could produce and fashion whatever kind of golden ornament he might desire;
even so, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples experience various kinds of psychic power:
being one, they become many; being many, they become one; they appear and disappear.
They disappear; they pass through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains without being obstructed, as if through space;
they dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; they walk on water without breaking the surface as if on earth;
and they travel cross-legged through the air like winged birds.
They even touch and stroke with their hands the moon and sun, so powerful and majestic;
they exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahma world.
And therein, many disciples of mine dwell having reached the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.

Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice such that, when my disciples have practiced it, they hear both kinds of sounds with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans—the sounds of gods and of men, whether far or near.

Just as, Udāyi, a powerful blower of a conch shell might easily make himself heard in all four directions; so too, Udāyi, my disciples, having practiced the way of practice I have proclaimed, hear both kinds of sounds with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans—the sounds of gods and of men, whether far or near.
In the same way, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the path of practice such that, when my disciples have practiced it,
they hear both kinds of sounds with the purified divine ear-element, which surpasses the human— the sounds of gods and of humans, whether far or near. And therein,
many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.

Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice such that, when my disciples practice accordingly, they understand the minds of other beings and other individuals by encompassing their minds with their own minds:
they understand a mind affected by lust as "a mind affected by lust," and they understand a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust."
They understand a mind with hatred as ‘a mind with hatred,’ and they understand a mind free from hatred as ‘a mind free from hatred’;
or they understand a mind with delusion as ‘a mind with delusion.’
They understand a mind free from delusion as ‘a mind free from delusion’;
they understand a contracted mind as ‘a contracted mind,’ and they understand a distracted mind as ‘a distracted mind.’
They understand an exalted mind as ‘exalted mind,’ or they understand an unexalted mind as ‘unexalted mind’;
or they understand a surpassable mind as ‘surpassable mind.’
They understand an unsurpassed mind as ‘an unsurpassed mind’;
they understand a concentrated mind as ‘a concentrated mind,’ and they understand an unconcentrated mind as ‘an unconcentrated mind.’
They understand a liberated mind as ‘a liberated mind,’ and they understand an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind.
Just as, Udāyi, a woman or a man— youthful, young, and fond of adornment— might look at their own reflection in a clear mirror, or...

Just as one examining the reflection of one’s own face in a clear, bright bowl of water would know it with its speck as "with a speck," or know it without a speck as "without a speck," even so, Udāyi,

I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice such that, by practicing it, my disciples understand the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing their minds with their own minds.
They understand a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," or a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust" ... pe ...
or a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred"... [and so on].
A mind free from hatred...
a mind with delusion...
or a mind free from delusion...
Whether the mind is contracted … or whether the mind is distracted … or whether the mind is exalted …
Or a mind that is not sublime … or a surpassable mind … or an unsurpassable mind …
... a concentrated mind ...
or an unconcentrated mind ...
or a liberated mind ...
Or they understand an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind.
And therein, moreover, many of my disciples dwell having reached mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, according to which my disciples, practicing accordingly, [realize] manifold states.
They recollect their past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births,
three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, and even many aeons of world-dissolution.
"Through many aeons of world-expansion and many aeons of world-contraction and expansion, [I recall:

'In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I arose elsewhere;
and there too I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, and such an experience of pleasure and pain.'"
‘Having had such a lifespan, passing away from there, he has reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
Just as, Udāyi, a man might go from his own village to another village, and from that village to yet another...
He might go to a village; from that village he might return to his own village. It would occur to him:
"I indeed went from my own village to another village; there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and remained silent thus;
from that village too I went to such-and-such a village; there also I stood thus, sat thus..."
‘I spoke thus, I remained silent thus; indeed, I have returned from that village to my own village.
In the same way, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path of practice, by practicing which my disciples recollect their manifold past lives, namely:
one birth... [as before] ...thus with their aspects and particulars, their manifold past lives.”
They recollect their past lives.
And therein, Udāyi, many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, such that when my disciples practice accordingly, by means of the divine [eye]...
With the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, they see beings passing away and being reborn—
lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and they understand how beings fare according to their karma:
"Alas, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind..."
Those noble ones who were possessed of such qualities, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views, at the breaking up of the body, after death,
have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell.
But these worthy beings, however, were possessed of good conduct of body, possessed of good conduct of speech, and possessed of good conduct of mind.
‘They do not revile the noble ones; they hold right view and undertake actions based on right view.

At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, they see beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate.
They understand beings according to their kamma.
Just as, Udāyi, there might be two houses with doors, and a man with sight standing in the middle might see people entering the house, leaving it, walking back and forth, and wandering about;
even so, Udāyi, the way of practice for my disciples has been declared by me, and how my disciples, practicing accordingly, [perceive] with the divine [eye].

With the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, they see beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; they understand how beings fare according to their kamma. ...
And there, moreover, many of my disciples dwell having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge.
Furthermore, Udāyi, I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice such that, by practicing it, my disciples—
through the destruction of the taints— realize for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
and having attained them, they dwell therein.

"Just as, Udāyi, there might be a lake in a mountain cleft—clear, serene, and undisturbed—and a man with good eyesight standing on the bank might see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, and schools of fish moving about or staying still.
It would occur to him: 'This lake is indeed clear, serene, and undisturbed; therein are these...'"
“Oysters, shells, gravel, and pebbles, as well as schools of fish, move about and remain still. In the same way, Udāyi,
I have proclaimed to my disciples the path of practice, such that by practicing it, my disciples— through the destruction of the taints—
have realized for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
They enter and abide therein.
And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and mastery of direct knowledge.
This, Udāyi, is the fifth quality by which my disciples honor, revere, esteem, and worship me; and having honored and revered me, they dwell in dependence upon me.

“Udāyin, these are the five qualities on account of which my disciples honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me; having honored me, revered me, and esteemed me, they dwell in dependence upon me.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Delighted, the wanderer Sakuludāyin rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Mahāsakuludāyisutta, the seventh, is finished.
